# Versioning

## The software development life cycle

![](images/lifecycle.png){fig-align="center" height="500"}

**→ *Software is not static!***

## Versions

Every part of the software you use is actively maintained. New features are added, bugs are fixed, and sometimes the way a function works *changes entirely*.

![](images/python-timeline.png){fig-align="center" height="200"}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
import random
population = {'A', 'B', 'C', 'D'}
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**In Python 3.10 and earlier:**
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
random.sample(population, 2)
```
```
['B', 'A']
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**The same code in Python 3.11+:**
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| error: true
random.sample(population, 2)
```
:::
:::

---

![](images/R-timeline.png){fig-align="center" height="200"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
df <- data.frame(
  group = c('A', 'A', 'B', 'B'),
  value = c(1, 2, 3, 4)
)
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**In R < 4.0:**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
class(df$group)
```

```
[1] "factor"
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**The same code in R 4.0+:**
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
class(df$group)
```

```
[1] "character"
```
:::
:::

---

This is normal (and mostly great!) — but it means:

❌ Code written in 2024 may not behave the same way in 2026

❌ A script that worked last week may break after an update

❌ Two researchers running the "same" code may get different results
